mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Illapa ‌place ​thunder, lightning, ​war ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Illapa ‌appears ​in ‌incan tradition ​as ​thunder, lightning, ​war. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Thunder", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and ‌Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ​and ‌later tradition-keepers ‌preserved ‌Illapa in ​ritual, ​text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The ​myths of ​Illapa ​survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ‌and ​later retellings. ‌Each ​version reflects ​the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Illapa ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

archaeology.body:

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Illapa, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​thunder ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Illapa** ​(*illapa*) — ‌Thunder, ‌Lightning, War ​· ​The thundering ​warrior ​of the ​Andes ‌— belongs ​to ​the ‌Incan tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ​"Thunder, Lightning, ​War". ​The name ​means ‌"Thunder"[^1].

**Illapa** ​is ‌the Inca ​god ‌of **thunder, ​lightning, ‌and war ​— ‌the storm ​warrior ​whose sling-stones ‌are ‌the ‌thunderbolts**. He ​drew ​the rain ‌from ​the celestial ​river ‌and hurled ​it ​earthward, patron ‌of ​soldiers and ‌of ​every field ​that ​waited for ​rain.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling ​**Illapa** ​and serves ‌its ‌temple at ‌[its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/illapa/). The ​displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed form ​itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *illapa* ​contains ‌the same ​letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics ‌or ​special encoding ‌is ‌claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Illapa** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "Thunder"[^1].

​The ​canonical ​spelling **Illapa** ​matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*illapa* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters, ​so no ​lost ‌diacritics ‌or encoding ‌transition ​is ​claimed. The ‌editorial ​work ​is to ‌fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, ​and keep ​the ​original ‌evidence visible. ‌The ​displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ‌computed ‌from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**i** → ​**I** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ‌**l** ​→ ​**l** — ​Same
- ‌**l** ​→ **l** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ‌— ‌Same
- **p** ​→ ​**p** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

meditation.body: Illapa ​teaches that ‌a storm ‌is ​**an armed ​presence, not ​a ​process**. The ​Andes live ‌under ​skies that ​can kill ‌a ​herder or ‌save a ​valley ‌in an ​afternoon; the ​Inca ​response was ​to give ​that ‌volatility a ​person, a ‌sling, ​and a ‌supply line. ​There ‌is a ​political reading ‌here ​— the ​storm god ‌is ‌also the ‌war god, ​and ​the empire ‌that fed ​him ​captives and ‌chicha was ​an ​empire that ‌understood force ​as weather: ‌overwhelming, ​directional, and ​answerable to ​ritual. ​But there ‌is a ‌homelier ​lesson too. ‌The thunderstone ​kept ​in a ‌farmhouse, the ‌cairn ‌at the ‌pass, the ​child ‌taught to ​count the ​gap ​between flash ‌and crack ​— ​these are ​technologies of ‌relationship ​with a ​dangerous sky. ​Where ‌other traditions ​explained thunder ‌as ​noise, the ‌Quechua tradition ​gave ‌it *aim* ‌— and ​therefore ​something one ​could address, ​placate, ‌and occasionally ‌petition for ​rain.[^1]
